{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Charles Frederick Wells''' (4 May 1937 in [[Atlanta, Georgia]] – 17 June 2017)<ref>Birth and Career Data from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=misterZ3r0 |title=Update on AbstractMath.org: a website that provided an introduction to advanced mathematics |url=https://www.reddit.com/r/learnmath/comments/6jhygc/update_on_abstractmathorg_a_website_that_provided/ |access-date=2 November 2024 |work=reddit/learnmath |date=26 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180322031150/https://www.reddit.com/r/learnmath/comments/6jhygc/update_on_abstractmathorg_a_website_that_provided/ |archive-date=22 March 2018 |quote=I am sorry to inform the community that Professor Charles Wells who ran the website as a free resource passed away on June 17, 2017. I received a reply to an email inquiring Professor Wells why the website was down. Here was the reply:  ''Hi Eugene... this Matt Wells, Charles' son. Sad to report that Dad died suddenly and peacefully on Saturday night. He left behind all of the instructions on how to fix the website, so we'll figure it out eventually. matt''}}</ref> was an American mathematician known for his fundamental contributions to [[category theory]]. He was Professor Emeritus of Mathematics at [[Case Western Reserve University]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cwru.edu/artsci/math/wells/home.html |title=Home page at CWRU |access-date=2012-02-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161231073212/http://www.cwru.edu/artsci/math/wells/home.html |archive-date=2016-12-31 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Wells taught there for about 35 years, with sabbatical interruptions at [[ETH Zurich|ETH Zürich]] (in mathematics) and [[Oxford University Computing Laboratory|Oxford University]] (in computing science). He had a research career in mathematics in [[finite fields]], [[group theory]] and [[category theory]]. In the last twenty years of this life he had also been interested in the [https://abstractmath.org/MM/MMLangMath.htm language of mathematics] and related issues concerning teaching and communicating abstract ideas.

==Publications==
In addition to his scholarly publications, Wells produced ''A Handbook of Mathematical Discourse,''<ref>Negative review: {{citation |last1=Krantz  |first1=Steven G. |date=September 2004 |title=Book Review: A Handbook of Mathematical Discourse|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200408/rev-krantz.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |volume=51 |issue=8 |pages=897–898 }}</ref><ref>Positive review: {{citation |last1=Selden |first1= Annie |date=February 27, 2014 |title=MAA Review: A Handbook of Mathematical Discourse |url=https://old.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/a-handbook-of-mathematical-discourse |journal=Mathematical Association of America Reviews }}</ref> which is a dictionary of words and concepts used by mathematicians that are easily misunderstood, explained in a way that laypersons can also appreciate.

As a life-long [[shape note]] singer, in 2002 Wells jointly compiled a tunebook called ''Oberlin Harmony,''<ref>Charles Wells, Chloe Maher, ''Oberlin Harmony'' (2002, Oberlin, Ohio). Incomplete table of contents given in: {{cite web |url=https://hymnary.org/hymnal/OH2002 |title=Oberlin Harmony |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=Hymnary.org |access-date=18 January 2020 }}</ref> which included some of his own compositions.
